requirement: The developer may need to include a landowner's property in the project's "footprint" and encumber it with a Wind Energy Land Agreement even though no physical project facilities will be located on the property.

When the developer wants to place on one landowner's property a substation or an O&M facility that will serve the entire wind energy project, the landowner may believe it is entitled to additional compensation for the added benefit to the developer and added burden on the owner and loss of usable property caused by construction of such a facility on its property.

The same may be true for transmission lines, collector lines, access and crane roads, and other features that remove land area from the landowner's continuing farm or other use or that preclude wind development by other competing developers even if no facilities at all are placed on its property.

Certain states, particularly in the Midwest, impose strict timelines that must be met to keep the Wind Energy Land Agreement in effect, and, depending on the state, development of the project must commence or commercial operations must begin within specified time periods, even if the Wind Energy Land Agreement contains a more flexible provision.

The developer may also reserve the right to further extend the term for additional renewal periods, often ranging from 20 to 30 years, and to "repower" all or part of the project at some point during the extended term or otherwise extend the life of the project.

The developer considering such a third-party arrangement would have to confirm whether, how, and under what conditions its Wind Energy Land Agreement allowed such third-party rights and what, if any, additional compensation and other obligations might be owed to the landowner.
scope: Wind farm projects with third-party storage facilities

requirement: Adding a series of electric car batteries removed from junked electric cars to a wind project, with a few per turbine (for instance) to offset imbalance issues, should not materially affect any other project facility or require extensive additional land or infrastructure.
scope: Wind farms with integrated energy storage

requirement: Specialized access roads, sometimes even requiring alterations to the public roads serving the project site. Development may not be possible if the access road serving the project area is a twisting, 15-foot-wide, private easement over adjacent lands owned by one or more third parties or the easement provides that it is limited to agricultural use or to certain times or seasons or other limited use.

An easement that is tied to (is appurtenant to) a particular parcel or parcels sought to be accessed and potentially developed cannot typically lawfully be used to access other parcels or areas, even if those other parcels or areas are adjacent to or accessible from the appurtenant (benefited) parcels.

Evaluate whether a subordination agreement is required, or if a nondisturbance and attornment agreement will suffice, and whether the prior lender or lessee will agree to provide such comfort to the wind developer.

The developer will want to ensure that the curative arrangements made with a tenant farmer, for instance, are consistent with the developer's obligations to the landowner under its site control agreement.

Evaluate whether a consent and crossing agreement is necessary, or if a modification of an existing easement, such as confining an otherwise blanket easement to a specific, limited location, will suffice (and be available).
scope: Existing easements encumbering the project lands

requirement: The Migratory Bird Treaty Act (MBTA) and Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act (Eagle Act) generally prohibit some form of 'take' (i.e., injury or killing) of protected species.
source: Migratory Bird Treaty Act (MBTA) and Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act (Eagle Act)

requirement: The Endangered Species Act (ESA) provides two mechanisms for obtaining permits for incidental take of protected species, including a formal section 7 consultation under the ESA, or a section 10 'incidental take permit' (ITP) that authorizes the take of a species that is 'incidental to, and not the purpose of, carrying out an otherwise lawful activity'.
An ITP must be accompanied by a Habitat Conservation Plan that receives U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service (FWS or the Service) approval.
Since 2009, Eagle Act regulations have provided a mechanism to secure eagle ITPs for take that is associated with, but not the purpose of, a particular activity.
source: Bald and Golden Eagle Protection Act (Eagle Act)

requirement: In 2013, the FWS issued its final Eagle Conservation Plan Guidance (ECPG) to promote compliance with the Eagle Act and provide in-depth guidance for conserving bald and golden eagles in the course of siting, constructing, and operating wind energy facilities.
Attempt to avoid sensitive habitats, consider mitigation for habitat impacts that cannot be avoided, and provide for soil conservation and any necessary erosion-control measures.
Lights on the turbines, which are typically required by the Federal Aviation Administration ("FAA") and the Department of Defense ("DOD"), can have nighttime visual impacts.
Associated substations and transmission lines can add to the visual impact of a wind project.
Mitigation for visual impacts typically includes painting turbines a neutral color that blends into the landscape.
Each state bordering the Atlantic Ocean or Pacific Ocean has jurisdiction over submerged lands out to three nautical miles offshore pursuant to the Submerged Lands Act of 1953.
scope: Offshore wind farms in state waters

requirement: Texas, Florida, and Louisiana have jurisdiction over submerged lands in the Gulf of Mexico out to nine nautical miles offshore.
scope: Offshore wind farms in state waters in the Gulf of Mexico

requirement: Beyond the state jurisdictional borders, jurisdiction to grant leases, rights-of-way (ROWs), and rights-of-use and easements (RUEs) on the Outer Continental Shelf (OCS) for most energy projects lies with the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM), a division of the U.S. Department of the Interior, pursuant to the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act as amended by the Energy Policy Act of 2005 (EPAct).
scope: Offshore wind farms in federal waters
source: Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act, Energy Policy Act of 2005

requirement: In the Great Lakes, each state has jurisdiction over submerged lands out to the center of each lake.
scope: Offshore wind farms in the Great Lakes

requirement: The PPA may require the seller to deliver energy to a specific point some distance from the plant, in which case the seller will be responsible for securing the required transmission to the delivery point, and the buyer will be responsible for obtaining the transmission required to take the energy at the delivery point.
Transmission ancillary services can be fairly costly and should be specifically allocated in the agreement.

In a VPPA, energy is not actually delivered to the offtaker. Instead, energy is typically sold into the energy market with which the project is interconnected at such point of interconnection. The settlement under the VPPA is typically at a different point on the system (often a hub or collection of nodes), which exposes Seller to basis risk between the point of interconnection and hub.

The PPA may require the purchaser to buy power from the turbines as they are installed, connected to the transmission grid, and made operational, even though the project as a whole has not achieved commercial operation.
The hedge does not always cover 100 percent of the energy anticipated to be produced by the wind

Transmission considerations can still play a key role, as the location of the wind plant may be such that it is on the wrong side of a grid congestion point, thus adversely affecting the market price of the power and thereby affecting the economics (and perhaps even the availability) of the hedge

The high-voltage work including the project substation, transmission lines, and in some cases interconnection facilities under a self-build election pursuant to the interconnection agreement, may be included in or part of a separate high-voltage contract.
scope: High-voltage components of the wind farm project

requirement: Federal tax law requires that investors put their dollars at risk in the project in order to claim the Production Tax Credit (PTC) benefits.
scope: Wind projects seeking to utilize the PTC

requirement: Tax equity structures rely largely on the principle of bifurcation, where the tax items of a partnership are allocated separately from the partner's respective cash flows and management rights.

In a partnership flip transaction, the allocation of cash and tax benefits under the operating agreement is structured such that the tax equity investor receives the majority of the tax benefits until they reach a target internal rate of return, at which point the allocation 'flips' and the sponsor receives the majority of the cash distributions.

An investor cannot claim any PTCs to offset taxable income if the PTCs in question were generated prior to the investor being an equity owner of the project. Such pre-investment PTCs are thus 'lost' in the sense that they have no value to the tax equity investors and hence are not part of the tax benefits monetized through the tax equity financing.
There is no established market for a typical development-stage loan, and terms vary widely among what are fundamentally bespoke deals.
scope: Development-stage financing for renewable energy projects

requirement: Many entities act as development financiers in order to claim a seat at the project table, for instance, entities interested in buying or funding the project if early-stage development proceeds to full construction, contractors looking to secure the project's EPC work, or turbine manufacturers looking to ensure their product is used in the project.
scope: Development-stage financing for renewable energy projects

requirement: In certain instances, development loans can also be a bridge to future funding, providing a quick, relatively low-cost transaction with minimal documentation; a very short tenor; little borrower flexibility without lender consent; a high interest rate; and a promise to grant the lender a right of first refusal to the next round of larger financing or, in the case of a strategic investor, the option to buy the project.
scope: Development-stage financing for renewable energy projects

requirement: Many early-stage investments involve collateral security and operational covenants securing a future payment (and are thus debt-like in their protections) without the payment obligation actually constituting indebtedness on the obligor's balance sheet.
scope: Early-stage financing for renewable energy projects

requirement: Lenders typically require lien waivers from contractors, subcontractors, and major equipment suppliers as a condition to each construction loan used to pay such counterparties, and the title company will require such lien waivers in order to issue a customary date-down endorsement to the title policy insuring the lender's security interest in the project.

A breach or default under any tax equity transaction document (in addition to a breach or default under any loan document or material project document, or any other event reasonably likely to have a material adverse effect on the project) will typically prevent the borrower from accessing any further construction loans.
scope: Wind projects with tax equity financing

requirement: Construction loans are often earmarked by tranches to refer to the expected source of repayment (for instance tax equity bridge loans as the bridge to a tax equity commitment). These tranches may have different features, including different interest rates or disbursement requirements.
scope: Wind projects with construction loans and tax equity financing

requirement: Following achievement of COD and completion of construction of a wind project, a sponsor will typically trade its restrictive and expensive construction debt for (or convert it into) permanent financing, allowing recoupment of invested capital.
scope: Wind projects after commercial operation date (COD)

requirement: Tax equity will seek to avoid taking any sponsor risk to the extent it can be avoided.

The property must be equipment that is used to produce electricity from wind. The property must be (1) tangible personal property or (2) other tangible property (not including a building or its structural components) that is an integral part of the wind facility.
The property must be eligible for depreciation or amortization deductions for federal income tax purposes.
The property must be part of a qualified facility that is located in the United States, is owned by the taxpayer seeking to claim the ITC, and the construction of which began before January 1, 2022.
The property cannot be part of a facility for which the PTC has been allowed.
The owner of the property must make an irrevocable election to claim the ITC.

The amount of the ITC is reduced by 20 percent in the case of any facility the construction of which began after December 31, 2016 and before January 1, 2018, 40 percent in the case of any facility the construction of which began after December 31, 2017 and before January 1, 2019, 60 percent in the case of any facility the construction of which began after December 31, 2018 and before January 1, 2020, and 40 percent in the case of any facility the construction of which began after December 31, 2019 and before January 1, 2022.
The ownership of the project assets in a single-purpose subsidiary enables a project lender to protect its collateral package from other creditors.
The isolation of the assets in a subsidiary simplifies the transaction when selling all or portions of the wind project.
Most transmission providers are subject to jurisdiction by FERC, and therefore transmission service agreements and generation interconnection agreements are generally subject to regulation by FERC.
scope: Transmission service agreements and generation interconnection agreements
source: FERC Order No. 2003 and FERC Order No. 2006

requirement: Interconnection to utilities exempt from FERC interconnection rules raises unique questions, which should be considered when selecting project sites.
scope: Interconnection to utilities exempt from FERC interconnection rules

requirement: FERC Order No. 2003 established standard interconnection procedures and a standard interconnection agreement for generators larger than 20 MW ("Large Generators").
FERC Order No. 2006 established standard interconnection procedures and a standard interconnection agreement for generators smaller than 20 MW.

The permitting process provides many opportunities to challenge a project. However, post-construction challengers must demonstrate that the operation of the wind power project violates some state or federal law and that a private lawsuit is authorized.

The theory behind a nuisance lawsuit in the context of a wind power project is that the project operator is using its land in a manner that 'substantially and unreasonably' interferes with a nearby property owner's ability to 'use and enjoy' his or her own property. Plaintiffs will allege that a wind power project creates too much noise, casts too much shadow or shadow flicker, or creates a visual impairment.
